distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for acute immune hemolysis caused by transfused red cells or red-cell-containing products, with clinical expression during transfusion or within the early post-transfusion window.
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: ABO-incompatible, minor-antigen alloantibody, complement-dominant, extravascular, intraoperative, obstetric, and massive-transfusion contexts are represented as mechanisms, context axes, and risk modifiers. FNHTR, TRALI, TACO, allergic/anaphylactic reaction, septic transfusion reaction, hyperhemolysis syndrome, and delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction are not part of this leaf and should be separate future manifolds or mimics.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may use recent transfusion exposure, timing during or shortly after transfusion, fever/chills, flank or back pain, hemoglobinuria or red-brown urine, jaundice, hemoglobin fall, LDH rise, low haptoglobin, bilirubin rise, AKI, shock, and DIC physiology. Final blood bank adjudication, repeat ABO/crossmatch, antibody identification, DAT/IAT, eluate, and compatibility investigation should be confirmatory or non-ranking unless explicitly available at the tested clinical stage.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Transfused red cells or red-cell-containing components expose the recipient to donor RBC antigens during an active transfusion episode.
Recipient anti-A/anti-B isoagglutinins or clinically significant alloantibodies bind antigens on transfused donor RBCs. This can reflect ABO error or minor-antigen incompatibility.

Antibody binding activates complement on transfused RBCs, causing abrupt intravascular lysis, free hemoglobin release, haptoglobin depletion, hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, inflammatory mediator release, and renal tubular heme toxicity.
Some alloantibody reactions clear incompatible transfused cells through macrophages in spleen and liver, producing hemoglobin fall, bilirubin rise, LDH rise, jaundice, and variable hemoglobinuria.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Acute cytokine, pain, and autonomic response
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Complement fragments, hemolysis mediators, pain, anxiety, and inflammatory signaling produce fever, chills, rigors, back or flank pain, tachycardia, nausea, and sometimes hypotension during the reaction.

Filtered free hemoglobin, heme toxicity, tubular casts, renal vasoconstriction, shock, and volume depletion can cause oliguria, anuria, creatinine rise, azotemia, metabolic acidosis, and dialysis need.

Severe intravascular hemolysis can activate coagulation, complement, nitric-oxide scavenging, endothelial injury, and systemic inflammation, producing DIC, bleeding, shock, respiratory decompensation, and multiorgan failure.
Destruction of transfused RBCs and ongoing bleeding or anemia lower oxygen-carrying capacity and can produce tachycardia, dyspnea, ischemia, syncope, or higher mortality in low-reserve patients.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: The disease cannot occur without a transfusion exposure, although transfusion alone is not sufficient for diagnosis.
Symptoms begin during or soon after transfusion in acute hemolytic reactions.
Mismatch becomes clinically active only when incompatible donor RBCs enter circulation.
ABO and some alloantibodies can fix complement and lyse donor RBCs abruptly.
Non-ABO alloantibodies can clear incompatible donor cells through macrophage Fc receptors.
Repeat blood grouping, crossmatch, antibody ID, eluate, or clerical investigation may identify the mismatch after the reaction.
DAT may be positive when donor cells coated with IgG or complement remain detectable, but it can be negative after rapid destruction.
Abrupt hemolysis during transfusion produces the acute reaction cluster.
Intravascular donor RBC lysis releases free hemoglobin.
Filtered free hemoglobin causes red, brown, or cola-colored urine.
Dipstick heme with few or no RBCs supports pigmenturia rather than ordinary hematuria.
Free hemoglobin consumes circulating haptoglobin.
LDH rises from intravascular red-cell destruction and tissue injury.
Destruction of transfused RBCs and ongoing anemia lower measured hemoglobin.
Hematocrit tracks hemoglobin loss.
Heme catabolism from extravascular clearance raises bilirubin.
Indirect bilirubin rises with hemolysis.
Bilirubin rise can produce scleral icterus or jaundice.
Fever can be an early sign of AHTR, though it is not specific and overlaps FNHTR and sepsis.
Current measured temperature may be elevated early but can normalize by transfer or after treatment.
Chills or rigors are common acute transfusion-reaction symptoms.
Flank pain is a classic hemolytic transfusion reaction symptom and may reflect renal capsular or ureteral pigment stress.
Back pain is a classic transfusion-reaction symptom.
Generalized aches can accompany the acute inflammatory reaction.
Headache is nonspecific but reported in some acute reactions.
Fever, pain, anxiety, anemia, and shock can increase heart rate.
Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal symptoms can occur in acute transfusion reactions but are nonspecific.
Heme pigment nephropathy and shock raise creatinine.
Azotemia rises with AKI and catabolic stress.
Oliguria or anuria reflects severe AKI.
Anuria is a severe form of pigment or shock-associated AKI.
Renal failure and shock can produce metabolic acidosis.
Metabolic acidosis lowers arterial or venous pH.
Hemoglobinuria and heme toxicity specifically increase hemolysis-related AKI hazard.
AHTR can produce clinically meaningful AKI or dialysis need.
Coagulation activation or consumption can lower platelets in severe AHTR.
DIC or consumptive coagulopathy can prolong PT/INR.
DIC can prolong aPTT.
Severe intravascular hemolysis can trigger DIC.
Severe reactions can cause hypotension.
Complement, cytokines, DIC, and hemolysis can produce shock.
Respiratory decompensation can occur from shock, pulmonary edema, or competing transfusion reactions; it is not specific for AHTR.
Anemia and shock can cause dyspnea.
Acute anemia can cause weakness and fatigue.
Anemia can produce pallor.
DIC can produce clinically important bleeding.
The larger the free-hemoglobin load, the higher the risk of pigment AKI.
Complement and hemolysis mediators can activate coagulation and shock pathways.
Complement and hemolysis mediator release drives fever, pain, and autonomic symptoms.
Severe pigment AKI and dialysis need increase mortality and morbidity.
Shock is an early lethal pathway.
DIC adds bleeding, thrombosis, and multiorgan failure risk.
Major bleeding can be fatal or worsen shock.
Higher hemoglobin lowers oxygen-delivery failure risk; falling hemoglobin increases hazard.

axes.shape_free_text: Recent transfusion of RBCs or a red-cell-containing product; exposure context, not proof of incompatibility.
Symptoms or signs begin during transfusion or soon after transfusion; strongest when minutes to hours.
Syndromic acute transfusion-reaction cluster with fever/chills, pain, dark urine, hypotension, or unexplained hemolysis.
Post-workup probability that repeat typing, crossmatch, antibody ID, eluate, or clerical investigation supports incompatible transfused RBC exposure.
DAT can be positive if donor or patient red cells are coated with IgG or complement; negative DAT does not exclude AHTR after rapid donor-cell destruction.
Red, brown, cola-colored, or visibly bloody urine in temporal association with hemolysis; may include hemoglobinuria or mixed hematuria.
Urinalysis heme strongly positive with few or no RBCs, supporting pigmenturia.
Free hemoglobin in plasma during intravascular hemolysis.
Hemoglobin may fall or fail to rise after transfusion because transfused RBCs are destroyed; baseline anemia often precedes the transfusion.
Hematocrit tracks hemoglobin fall.
LDH rises with hemolysis and tissue injury; abrupt high values support active hemolysis.
Low or undetectable haptoglobin from free hemoglobin binding.
Total bilirubin rises with hemolysis and may include direct fraction during critical illness.
Indirect bilirubin rises from heme catabolism.
Direct bilirubin can rise with severe illness, hemolysis-associated hepatic stress, pregnancy/postoperative context, or mixed cholestasis; less specific than indirect bilirubin.
Scleral icterus or jaundice during hemolysis.
Subjective or documented fever during the acute reaction.
Measured temperature; can be elevated early but normal after transfer or under anesthesia.
Chills or rigors during acute reaction; overlaps FNHTR and sepsis.
Flank pain during acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
Back pain during transfusion reaction.
Generalized aches or myalgia during systemic reaction; nonspecific.
Headache during transfusion reaction or AKI context; nonspecific.
Nausea or vomiting during acute reaction; nonspecific.
Tachycardia may reflect fever, pain, shock, or anemia; normal heart rate does not exclude AHTR.
MAP may remain normal in mild cases or fall in severe shock.
Respiratory rate can rise with pain, fever, shock, pulmonary edema, or acidosis.
Oxygen saturation is often normal in isolated AHTR but can fall with shock, pulmonary edema, or a separate TRALI/TACO mimic.
Stress leukocytosis may occur but WBC is nonspecific.
Platelets may be normal, low from DIC/consumption, diluted, or affected by comorbid bleeding/surgery.
Creatinine rises with hemoglobinuric AKI or shock; may be normal in mild cases.
BUN rises with AKI, hypovolemia, catabolic stress, or bleeding.
Daily urine output; low values encode oliguria/anuria from pigment AKI.
Clinical anuria or near-anuria after transfusion.
Sodium may vary with AKI and volume status; not core-specific.
Potassium can rise with hemolysis, transfusion load, or AKI, but may be normal.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from AKI or shock.
Arterial or venous pH can fall with metabolic acidosis from renal failure or shock.
INR may be normal or prolonged if DIC develops.
aPTT may be normal or prolonged if DIC develops.
Hazard of DIC or clinically important consumptive coagulopathy from severe intravascular hemolysis.
Hazard of clinically important bleeding from DIC, surgery, obstetric hemorrhage, or anticoagulation context.
Hazard of hypotensive shock during severe reaction.
AKI hazard specifically tied to intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, heme toxicity, and pigment casts.
General clinically meaningful AKI or dialysis hazard from AHTR, shock, pigment nephropathy, or baseline renal vulnerability.
Dyspnea from anemia, shock, volume overload, or a separate pulmonary transfusion mimic; nonspecific.
Weakness or fatigue from anemia or renal failure.
Pallor from anemia.
Peripheral edema from AKI, pregnancy, fluid loading, or volume overload; not specific for AHTR.
Lifespan-only mortality hazard for acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, driven by shock, DIC, AKI, severe anemia, and multiorgan failure. This is the only derived hazard for this leaf.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: The temporal anchor only has meaning when a transfusion exposure occurred.
Dark urine during or soon after transfusion is a high-value AHTR signal.
Free hemoglobin binds and depletes haptoglobin.
When haptoglobin is depleted, free hemoglobin is more likely to appear in urine.
LDH and bilirubin are both downstream of hemolysis, though timing and compartments differ.
Hemoglobinuria is the visible marker of pigment reaching renal tubules.
Oliguria or anuria increases AKI severity hazard.
Low MAP is central to shock physiology.
Severe AKI and dialysis need worsen survival.
Shock is a dominant early death pathway.
DIC adds fatal bleeding, thrombosis, and multiorgan failure risk.

treatments.treatment_name: Immediate cessation of transfusion with IV access maintained
treatments.role: remove ongoing incompatible antigen exposure and preserve resuscitation access

treatments.treatment_name: Blood bank reaction workup and compatible product control
treatments.role: identify mismatch, quarantine implicated products, prevent repeat incompatible exposure, and guide antigen-negative compatible support

treatments.treatment_name: Isotonic fluid, diuresis strategy, and renal protection
treatments.role: support renal perfusion and urine flow during pigment nephropathy risk while avoiding volume overload

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal protection requires perfusion support when shock is present.
Aggressive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema or TACO-like physiology.

treatments.role: restore perfusion when hypotension or shock develops

treatments.treatment_name: Renal replacement therapy for severe AKI
treatments.role: control uremia, electrolyte disturbance, acidosis, and volume overload when pigment AKI is severe
support coagulation and hemostasis when severe hemolysis triggers consumptive coagulopathy or bleeding

treatments.treatment_name: Antigen-negative compatible RBC support when oxygen delivery requires transfusion
treatments.role: restore oxygen delivery when anemia or bleeding remains dangerous after the implicated product is stopped

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Compatible product selection depends on blood bank findings and urgency.

present.clinical_rationale: Transfusion exposure is necessary but not sufficient; the temporal and hemolysis axes decide whether the exposure is explanatory.
AHTR is an acute transfusion-timed process, but timing alone must not override absent hemolysis evidence.
Confirmed incompatible unit or clinically significant antibody strongly supports this leaf when available at the tested stage.
Prior antigen exposure increases probability of clinically significant alloantibodies.
Larger antigen and hemolysis load increases AKI, DIC, shock, and mortality risk.
Anesthesia masks subjective symptoms, so hemoglobinuria, hypotension, bleeding, and labs become more visible signals.
Renal reserve and perfusion modify pigment-nephropathy severity.
Obstetric bleeding and peripartum physiology modify volume, coagulation, and renal risk while remaining context rather than a separate disease name.
The same hemoglobin drop is less tolerated when baseline reserve is low.

supportive_care.description: Stop the transfusion, keep IV access with normal saline, verify patient and unit identity, notify transfusion medicine, return product/tubing, and send required blood and urine samples.

Trend hemoglobin, plasma color or free hemoglobin when available, LDH, haptoglobin, total and indirect bilirubin, creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, acid-base status, urine color, urine heme/RBC pattern, and urine output.
Monitor blood pressure, perfusion, oxygenation, lactate when available, platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, bleeding, and need for ICU-level support.
Quarantine implicated products and avoid further transfusion until transfusion medicine directs compatible, antigen-negative, or emergency least-incompatible strategy.

Evaluate fever-only, allergic symptoms, acute hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, bacterial contamination, and delayed hemolysis as possible FNHTR, allergic/anaphylactic reaction, TRALI, TACO, septic transfusion reaction, or DHTR rather than forcing them into this leaf.

quality_notes: Pure disease-name distillation: no subtype or mimic was included in the disease name.
No manually assigned clinical ranking-label fields are used.
Blood bank final adjudication axes are modeled as diagnostic context and should stay non-ranking in presentation-only case tests unless available at that stage.
